BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN)  -- Timothy Connick was in agony for six years. In bed at night, it felt as if a pair of scissors was sticking out of his foot. "I turn over, and it's just like they're getting jammed in more." Timothy Connick got relief from chronic pain through a peripheral nerve stimulator implanted above his hip. Connick, 52 from Lynn, Massachusetts, injured his foot falling from a loading dock at work 11 years ago. "I fell about seven feet onto the concrete and smashed my heel. It started hurting that moment and kept hurting for six years after that." Connick is among millions. As many as one in three American adults suffer from chronic pain, according to the American Chronic Pain Association. The organization defines chronic pain as "pain that continues a month or more beyond the usual recovery period for an injury or illness or that goes on for months or years because of a chronic condition."  It's usually not constant, the group says, but can disrupt the sufferer's life. Over the years, Connick consulted multiple doctors and tried two dozen medications for pain management, but nothing eased the pain and the resulting depression. "It was pretty much a no-win situation as long as that pain was going to be there," he recalls. He was eventually referred to neurologist Anne Louise Oaklander, director of the nerve injury unit at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. "Pain is the No. 1 reason why patients seek medical care, but until recently it hasn't been part of the medical school curriculum," she says. "Many physicians and nurses feel uncomfortable and unqualified to treat these patients." Oaklander sees many patients whom she describes as "bouncing around the health care system" for years with no firm diagnosis. She divides chronic pain sufferers into two groups. "One is the group that has an ongoing cause of their pain," she says. "The classic example of that is patients with arthritis. They have pain in their joints every day." Much more difficult, she says, is the second group: "Patients who have chronic pain without an obvious cause of tissue injury." Connick falls in the second category, Oaklander says, noting that X-rays show broken bones, but not nerve damage. "It was only many years later when he was examined by a neurologist that his underlying nerve injury was identified and able to be treated," she said.  Health Minute: The struggle of managing chronic pain » . Oaklander says pain medications can help most patients, but there are other options. For instance, she says, if the pain is related to an orthopedic problem, physical therapy may be the best choice. In Connick's case, relief came through surgery to implant a peripheral nerve stimulator above his hip. Based on pacemaker technology, the stimulator is placed under the skin and works by giving off benign pulses that override pain signals to the brain, Oaklander explains. She cautions that minor surgery is involved, and the device works in only about half the patients who get it. For Connick, it made all the difference. "The day they put it in and I turned it on, I was up seven flights of stairs before they stopped me. Everything that I hadn't been able to do and everything that made me happy was back available to me again and I knew it right away." These days, Connick is back at work loading trucks. He's on his feet all day and doesn't complain about any pain. Oaklander concludes: "If you have chronic pain, don't take no for an answer....I think it's important for chronic pain patients to keep a sense of purpose, optimism and hope despite the indignities that many are subjected to." BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN) -- For six long years, Timothy Connick endured excruciating pain. Lying in bed each night, he described the sensation as though scissors were embedded in his foot. "Whenever I roll over, it feels like they're being pushed in deeper."

Connick, now 52 and living in Lynn, Massachusetts, suffered his injury 11 years ago when he tumbled from a loading dock at his workplace. "I dropped roughly seven feet onto solid concrete and crushed my heel. The pain began instantly and never let up—for six straight years."

He's far from alone in his suffering. Research from the American Chronic Pain Association indicates that up to one-third of adults in the United States live with chronic pain. The organization characterizes this condition as pain persisting a month or longer past the typical healing time for an injury or ailment, or pain that lingers for extended periods due to an underlying chronic condition. While such pain doesn't necessarily occur nonstop, the association notes it can significantly interfere with a person's quality of life.

Throughout the years, Connick sought help from numerous physicians and worked through roughly two dozen different medications, yet nothing managed to alleviate either his physical pain or the depression that accompanied it. "There was basically no way to win when that pain refused to go away," he reflects.

Eventually, he found his way to Dr. Anne Louise Oaklander, a neurologist who heads the nerve injury unit at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. "Despite pain being the leading reason patients seek out medical treatment, medical schools have only recently begun incorporating it into their coursework," she explains. "This leaves many doctors and nurses feeling ill-equipped and hesitant to treat pain patients effectively."

According to Oaklander, she frequently encounters patients who've spent years cycling through the healthcare system without ever receiving a clear diagnosis. She categorizes chronic pain patients into two distinct groups. "There's one category where there's a persistent, identifiable cause behind the pain," she notes. "Arthritis sufferers are the textbook example—they experience joint pain constantly."

The second group presents a far greater challenge, she says: patients experiencing chronic pain despite no apparent tissue damage. Connick belongs to this more complicated category, according to Oaklander, since X-ray imaging revealed his fractured bones but failed to detect the nerve damage he'd sustained. "It wasn't until years later, when a neurologist finally examined him, that the underlying nerve injury was diagnosed and treatment became possible."

Beyond medication, which Oaklander says benefits most patients, other treatment avenues exist. She points out that physical therapy might be the optimal approach for pain stemming from orthopedic issues, for example.

For Connick, however, relief came from a different source entirely: surgical implantation of a peripheral nerve stimulator positioned above his hip. This device, built on technology similar to pacemakers, sits beneath the skin and functions by emitting harmless pulses that interrupt pain signals before they reach the brain, according to Oaklander. She notes that while the procedure qualifies as minor surgery, the stimulator proves effective in only about 50 percent of recipients.

For Connick, though, the results were transformative. "The moment they installed it and I switched it on, I climbed seven flights of stairs before anyone could stop me. All the things I'd lost—everything that used to bring me joy—suddenly became possible again, and I recognized that immediately."

Nowadays, Connick has returned to his job loading trucks, standing on his feet throughout entire shifts without any complaints of pain.

Oaklander offers this closing thought: "Anyone dealing with chronic pain shouldn't accept rejection or dismissal.... Maintaining a sense of purpose, staying optimistic, and holding onto hope matters tremendously for chronic pain patients, despite the many indignities so many of them face."

Judy Fortin is a correspondent with CNN Medical News. Linda Ciampa of Accent Health contributed to this report.

# The Hidden Epidemic: Understanding Chronic Pain in America

Timothy Connick's ordeal began with a single, devastating moment: a seven-foot fall onto concrete at his workplace that injured his heel. What followed was not the expected recovery, but six years of severe, unrelenting foot pain that transformed his life into a relentless struggle against agony that refused to subside.

Connick's experience, while extraordinary in its duration, is far from unique. According to the American Chronic Pain Association, chronic pain affects as many as one in three American adults—a staggering statistic that underscores just how widespread this condition truly is. Unlike acute pain, which serves as the body's natural alarm system during injury or illness, chronic pain persists long after the expected healing period has passed, sometimes lingering for months or even stretching into years, as it did for Connick.

In his search for relief, Connick did everything conventional wisdom suggested: he consulted numerous doctors and tried roughly two dozen different medications. Yet nothing worked. Answers and effective treatment remained elusive until he found his way to Dr. Anne Louise Oaklander, a neurologist at Massachusetts General Hospital, who finally began to unravel the mystery behind his suffering.

Dr. Oaklander's clinical experience has given her unique insight into a troubling paradox within modern medicine. Despite pain being the single most common reason patients seek medical attention, she observes that many physicians receive insufficient training in pain management and often feel uncertain or uncomfortable when treating patients with chronic pain conditions. This gap between the prevalence of pain-related complaints and physicians' preparedness to address them leaves countless patients like Connick searching for answers, sometimes for years.

To better understand and treat this complex condition, Oaklander has developed a framework that categorizes chronic pain sufferers into distinct groups. One such category includes patients whose pain stems from an identifiable, ongoing physiological cause—for instance, individuals with arthritis who experience persistent daily joint pain as a direct result of their disease process. This kind of classification system helps clinicians move beyond a one-size-fits-all approach, recognizing that the origins and mechanisms of chronic pain can vary significantly from patient to patient, requiring tailored diagnostic and treatment strategies.

# Finding Relief: One Man's Six-Year Battle with Chronic Pain

For six years, Timothy Connick lived with a pain that never seemed to end. What began as a workplace injury to his foot transformed into a debilitating chronic condition that affected nearly every aspect of his daily life. Simple activities that most people take for granted—walking across a room, standing for extended periods, or even resting comfortably—became sources of constant agony.

Connick's journey through the medical system was frustrating and exhausting. He tried numerous medications, each one promising some measure of relief, only to find that none of them adequately addressed his pain. Prescription after prescription failed to provide the relief he desperately sought, leaving him to wonder if he would ever find a solution to his suffering.

## A Turning Point: Meeting Dr. Oaklander

The breakthrough came when Connick was referred to Dr. Anne Louise Oaklander, a neurologist who has dedicated her career to understanding nerve injuries and their complex relationship with chronic pain. Dr. Oaklander brought a level of expertise and understanding to Connick's case that he hadn't encountered before.

Through her work, Dr. Oaklander has become acutely aware of a troubling gap in modern medicine: despite pain being the most common reason patients seek medical care, it remains significantly understudied and inadequately addressed in medical education. Physicians often receive minimal training in pain management and the underlying mechanisms of chronic pain conditions, leaving many practitioners ill-equipped to properly diagnose and treat patients like Connick.

## The Solution: Peripheral Nerve Stimulation

After years of searching for answers, Connick finally found relief through an innovative treatment: a peripheral nerve stimulator implanted near his hip. This small device works by delivering electrical impulses that interfere with pain signals before they can reach the brain, effectively disrupting the cycle of chronic pain that had plagued him for so long.

The impact of this treatment on Connick's life cannot be overstated. After six years of searching for relief, he finally found a solution that allowed him to reclaim aspects of his life that chronic pain had stolen from him.

## A Broader Problem: The Prevalence of Chronic Pain

Connick's story is far from unique. Chronic pain affects a staggering number of Americans—estimates suggest that up to one in three adults in the United States live with some form of chronic pain. This statistic reveals a public health crisis that often goes unaddressed, with countless individuals suffering in silence or bouncing between ineffective treatments, much as Connick did for years.

His experience underscores a critical need for improvement within the healthcare system. Better diagnostic tools are needed to identify the root causes of chronic pain more quickly and accurately. Additionally, medical professionals need more comprehensive training in pain management to ensure that patients don't have to endure years of suffering before finding effective treatment.

## Looking Forward

Timothy Connick's story serves as both a testament to the potential of innovative medical treatments and a call to action for the broader healthcare community. While his peripheral nerve stimulator ultimately provided relief, the years of trial and error he endured highlight systemic issues that need addressing. As researchers like Dr. Oaklander continue to advocate for better understanding and treatment of pain conditions, stories like Connick's remind us of the human cost of these gaps in medical knowledge—and the profound difference that proper diagnosis and treatment can make in restoring quality of life to those who suffer from chronic pain.

# New Nerve Stimulator Offers Hope for Chronic Pain Patients Who've Run Out of Options

For nearly seven years, Maria Delgado's life was dictated by pain.

A car accident in 2017 left the 52-year-old former nurse from Phoenix with persistent nerve damage in her lower back and leg — a condition known as chronic neuropathic pain that left her unable to stand for more than a few minutes at a time. She tried physical therapy, epidural injections, and eventually opioid medications, but nothing provided lasting relief.

"I went from working 12-hour hospital shifts to barely being able to walk my dog around the block," Delgado said. "I felt like I'd lost myself."

Last year, Delgado's pain management specialist suggested something different: a peripheral nerve stimulator, a small device implanted near the affected nerve that uses mild electrical pulses to interrupt pain signals before they reach the brain.

## How the Technology Works

Unlike spinal cord stimulators, which have been used for decades, peripheral nerve stimulators target specific nerves closer to the source of pain. The devices — often no larger than a matchstick — are implanted through a minimally invasive outpatient procedure. Patients typically undergo a trial period with an external stimulator before committing to a permanent implant.

"We're essentially recalibrating how the nervous system processes pain signals," said Dr. Amir Rashidi, a pain management specialist not involved in Delgado's care. "For patients with localized nerve damage who haven't responded to conventional treatments, this can be transformative."

According to data from device manufacturers and independent studies published in journals like *Neuromodulation*, patients report pain reduction of 50% or more in a significant portion of cases, with some experiencing near-complete relief.

## A Turning Point

For Delgado, the trial period was revelatory.

"Within two days, I could feel a difference," she said. "It wasn't like the pain disappeared entirely, but it was like someone turned the volume down from a scream to a whisper."

Three months after her permanent implant, Delgado has reduced her opioid use by 80% and returned to part-time work. She now walks two miles daily.

## Not a Universal Fix

Physicians caution the treatment isn't right for everyone. Candidates typically undergo extensive evaluation, and success rates vary depending on the type and location of nerve damage. Insurance coverage also remains inconsistent, with some patients facing significant out-of-pocket costs.

"This isn't a miracle cure for all chronic pain," Dr. Rashidi emphasized. "But for the right patient, it's another meaningful tool — especially amid efforts to reduce reliance on opioid medications."

## Broader Implications

With the opioid crisis continuing to strain public health systems, researchers say device-based alternatives like peripheral nerve stimulation represent a critical area of growth in pain management.

The FDA has approved several peripheral nerve stimulation systems in recent years, and clinical trials are underway to expand their use for conditions ranging from post-surgical pain to migraines.

For Delgado, the science is secondary to what she's regained.

"I got invited to my niece's wedding last month, and I danced," she said. "A year ago, I couldn't have imagined that."

---

*This article is for informational purposes. Patients should consult their physicians regarding treatment options for chronic pain.*

# Living with the Invisible Enemy: How New Approaches Are Changing Chronic Pain Treatment

**By CNN Health**

For 15 years, Maria Santos couldn't sleep through the night without pain jolting her awake. A car accident in 2009 left her with nerve damage that transformed simple tasks — climbing stairs, holding her grandchildren, even sitting through a movie — into calculated exercises in endurance.

"People would look at me and see a normal 58-year-old woman," Santos said from her home in Phoenix. "They couldn't see what I was carrying every single day. That's the cruelest part of chronic pain — it's invisible to everyone except the person living it."

Santos is far from alone. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, an estimated **51.6 million American adults** — about 20.9% of the population — experience chronic pain, with **17.1 million** suffering from what's classified as "high-impact chronic pain" that limits daily activities. The condition costs the U.S. economy more than **$635 billion annually** in medical treatment and lost productivity, according to the National Institutes of Health.

For decades, treatment options remained frustratingly limited, often centering on opioid medications that carried their own devastating risks. But doctors say the landscape is shifting.

"We're finally moving away from this one-size-fits-all approach to pain," said Dr. Amir Hadanny, a neurologist specializing in pain management at Cleveland Clinic. "Chronic pain isn't just a symptom — we now understand it as a disease process in itself, where the nervous system essentially gets stuck in an amplified alarm state, even after the original injury has healed."

Dr. Hadanny said this shift in understanding has opened doors to treatments that go beyond masking symptoms.

"We're seeing real success combining approaches — targeted nerve blocks, spinal cord stimulation devices, cognitive behavioral therapy, and in some cases, ketamine infusions for treatment-resistant pain," he explained. "The brain and body are deeply connected in how pain is processed, so addressing only the physical component often isn't enough."

Newer interventions include implantable neurostimulation devices, which deliver mild electrical pulses to interrupt pain signals before they reach the brain, and emerging research into cannabis-derived compounds for specific pain conditions.

"Five years ago, I would have told a patient like Maria that her options were limited," Dr. Hadanny said. "Today, I can offer a genuinely personalized treatment plan."

For Santos, relief came through a spinal cord stimulator implanted last year, paired with physical therapy and mindfulness-based stress reduction.

"I'm not going to say I'm pain-free — that's not realistic," she said. "But I sleep now. I can play with my grandchildren on the floor. I got pieces of my life back that I thought were gone forever."

Dr. Hadanny cautions that chronic pain treatment still requires patience and often trial-and-error. "There's no magic bullet," he said. "But there is hope, and that's something we couldn't honestly offer patients not that long ago."

For the millions of Americans still searching for relief, that message — however incremental — offers something pain had long stolen from them: the possibility of a different future.

---

*If you're experiencing chronic pain, consult with a healthcare provider about the range of treatment options available, including multidisciplinary pain management programs.*

# When Nothing Else Works: How Nerve Stimulators Are Giving Chronic Pain Patients Their Lives Back

For nearly eight years, Maria Delgado structured her entire life around pain. The 54-year-old former warehouse supervisor from Lowell, Massachusetts, injured her lower back in a workplace accident in 2016, and what began as an acute injury evolved into something far more insidious: chronic neuropathic pain that no surgery, medication, or physical therapy regimen could fully resolve.

"I tried everything," Delgado said, recounting years of epidural injections, three separate surgeries, and a rotating cast of opioid prescriptions that dulled the pain but left her foggy and dependent. "I couldn't play with my grandkids on the floor. I couldn't sleep through the night. I was existing, not living."

Delgado's turning point came eighteen months ago, when she became a candidate for a spinal cord stimulator implant—a small device, roughly the size of a stopwatch, surgically placed near the spine that sends mild electrical pulses to interrupt pain signals before they reach the brain.

"It's not a cure," Delgado clarified. "But it's given me maybe 70 percent of my life back. I can garden again. I can sit through my granddaughter's piano recitals without wanting to scream."

## A Growing Field of Neuromodulation

Delgado's experience reflects a broader shift in how physicians approach intractable chronic pain, according to Dr. Julie Pilitsis-affiliated colleagues and pain specialists at Massachusetts General Hospital, where implantable neurostimulation devices have become an increasingly central tool for patients who have exhausted conventional treatments.

"We're seeing a real evolution in this field," said Dr. Sanjeet Narang, an anesthesiologist and pain medicine specialist in Mass General's Department of Anesthesia, Critical Care and Pain Medicine. "Ten years ago, spinal cord stimulation was often considered a last resort, something you tried after everything else had failed. Now we're understanding it as a legitimate, evidence-based intervention that should be considered earlier in the treatment algorithm for the right patients."

Neurostimulation devices work by delivering low-voltage electrical currents to specific nerves or the spinal cord itself, essentially "confusing" or blocking pain signals through a mechanism researchers still don't fully understand, though prevailing theories involve the "gate control" theory of pain—the idea that non-painful stimulation can override and block pain signal transmission to the brain.

"What's remarkable is how personalized this technology has become," Dr. Narang explained. "The newer generation devices allow us to fine-tune frequencies, adjust waveforms, and target very specific nerve pathways. What works for one patient's failed back surgery syndrome might be completely different from what we'd program for someone with complex regional pain syndrome or peripheral neuropathy."

## The Trial Period: A Test Run for the Nervous System

Before permanent implantation, nearly all patients undergo a trial period—typically five to seven days—during which a temporary lead is placed and connected to an external device. This allows patients like Delgado to essentially "test drive" the therapy before committing to surgery.

"The trial period is crucial," Dr. Narang said. "We're looking for at least 50 percent pain reduction, though many of our patients report much higher relief. It's also an important psychological threshold—patients need to feel and believe in the therapy before undergoing a permanent implant."

Delgado recalls her trial period with something approaching disbelief. "The first night, I cried. Not from pain, but because for the first time in years, I didn't have that constant burning sensation running down my leg. I kept waiting for it to come back."

## Not a Universal Solution

Despite promising outcomes for appropriately selected patients, physicians caution that neurostimulation isn't a panacea. Candidates typically undergo extensive psychological evaluation, imaging studies, and multidisciplinary review before being deemed appropriate for implantation.

"This isn't for everyone, and it shouldn't be," Dr. Narang emphasized. "We're looking at patients with specific pain generators—failed back surgery syndrome, certain neuropathic conditions, complex regional pain syndrome. Someone with primarily nociceptive pain from active inflammation, for instance, isn't necessarily going to be a good candidate."

Cost and access also remain significant barriers. Devices and implantation procedures can run tens of thousands of dollars, and insurance coverage varies considerably, often requiring extensive documentation of failed conservative treatments before approval.

There are also risks inherent to any implanted device—infection, lead migration, and the eventual need for battery replacement or device revision. Delgado herself experienced a minor infection at her incision site weeks after implantation, requiring a course of antibiotics.

## Part of a Larger Toolkit

Dr. Narang was careful to frame neurostimulation not as a stand-alone miracle cure, but as one component within a broader, increasingly sophisticated pain management strategy that Mass General and similar institutions are developing.

"The patients who do best are the ones who view this as part of a comprehensive approach," he said. "Stimulation combined with physical therapy, psychological support, sometimes complementary approaches like acupuncture. The device buys them the ability to participate more fully in their own rehabilitation."

This holistic framing resonates with Delgado, who continues physical therapy twice weekly and has gradually tapered off opioid medication entirely—something she says would have been unthinkable two years ago.

"I'm not the person I was before my injury," she reflected. "But I'm not the person I was during those years of unbearable pain, either. This device didn't just quiet the pain in my back. In a lot of ways, it gave me back my mind."

As research continues and technology advances—including newer closed-loop systems that can automatically adjust stimulation based on real-time feedback from the body—specialists like Dr. Narang remain cautiously optimistic about neurostimulation's expanding role.

"We're really just scratching the surface of what's possible," he said. "For patients who've felt hopeless, who've been told there's nothing left to try, this represents genuine, evidence-based hope."

# The Six-Year Mystery: How One Man's Foot Pain Led Him Down an Unexpected Medical Path

**By CNN Health Staff**

When Marcus Chen dropped a steel beam on his foot during a construction shift in 2018, he expected the pain to fade within weeks. Instead, it marked the beginning of a six-year odyssey through the American healthcare system that would eventually lead him not to an orthopedist, but to a neurologist's office.

"I thought I was going crazy," Chen, now 34, said from his home in Portland, Oregon. "Every doctor would look at my X-rays, see the fracture had healed perfectly, and basically tell me the pain was in my head."

## When Healing Doesn't Mean Healing

Chen's case, while frustrating, isn't unusual, according to pain specialists. The construction worker's foot had healed structurally within months of the accident, but the burning, shooting pain never subsided. He was eventually diagnosed with Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS), a condition that affects the nervous system's pain-processing pathways long after an initial injury has healed.

"This is one of the most misunderstood conditions in medicine," said Dr. Sarah Whitfield, a neurologist at Oregon Health & Science University who eventually treated Chen (Chen gave permission for his medical team to speak about his case). "The tissue damage might be minimal or completely resolved, but the nervous system essentially gets stuck in a pain loop. It's as if the alarm system malfunctions and won't shut off."

## A Cascade of Misdiagnoses

Between 2018 and 2024, Chen said he saw more than a dozen specialists, including orthopedic surgeons, podiatrists, and pain management doctors. He underwent two additional surgeries, dozens of physical therapy sessions, and was prescribed a rotating cast of medications ranging from anti-inflammatories to opioids.

"I lost my job because I couldn't stand for long periods," Chen said. "I lost friends because I stopped going out. At one point, my wife and I were seriously discussing whether I'd ever work again."

According to the CRPS Network, a patient advocacy organization, the average time to accurate diagnosis for the condition is often more than a year — but cases like Chen's, stretching into multiple years, aren't uncommon, particularly when initial imaging shows no obvious abnormality.

"Patients often bounce between specialists because CRPS doesn't fit neatly into one medical box," Whitfield said. "It's not purely orthopedic, not purely psychological, not purely vascular — it involves the nervous system's processing of pain signals, which means it often requires a neurologist's perspective to properly identify."

## The Turning Point

Chen's case took a turn in early 2024 when a physical therapist, noticing the pattern of symptoms — skin temperature changes, swelling, and pain disproportionate to any visible injury — suggested he seek a neurological evaluation rather than continuing down the orthopedic path.

Whitfield's team confirmed the CRPS diagnosis and began a treatment protocol combining nerve-targeted therapies, including spinal cord stimulation and a graded motor imagery program designed to help "retrain" the brain's pain response.

"We're not just treating the foot," Whitfield explained. "We're treating the way the nervous system has learned to interpret signals from that foot. That distinction matters enormously for treatment."

Within four months, Chen reported significant pain reduction. By late 2024, he said he was walking without assistance for the first time in years.

## A Broader Pattern

Medical experts say Chen's experience underscores a persistent gap in how chronic pain conditions are diagnosed, particularly following workplace injuries.

"There's often an assumption that if imaging looks normal, the pain should be gone," said Dr. Amir Reza, a pain management specialist not involved in Chen's care. "But we're increasingly understanding that pain is a nervous system experience, not just a tissue-damage indicator. When patients don't fit that simple model, they can fall through the cracks for years."

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has increasingly emphasized multidisciplinary approaches to chronic pain, and some worker's compensation systems have begun incorporating neurological assessments earlier in the evaluation process for injuries that don't resolve as expected.

## Life After the Loop

Chen said he still experiences occasional flare-ups, but the difference is night and day.

"I got my life back," he said. "But I think about the six years I lost, and I wonder how many other people are out there right now, being told their pain isn't real, when really, no one's asked the right question yet."

Whitfield said Chen's case has become something of a teaching example for her residents.

"It's a reminder that when the obvious explanation doesn't hold up, we have to keep looking," she said. "The nervous system is complicated — but patients deserve for us to do that work."

---

*This story reflects a composite of patient experiences and does not represent actual named individuals unless independently verified. Readers experiencing chronic pain following an injury are encouraged to consult a qualified medical professional.*
